subject: English
description: Common grammar errors and their corrections

questions.stem: Choose the sentence that is grammatically correct.

options.option_text: Each of the students have completed the assignment.
Each of the students has completed the assignment.
Each of the students are completed the assignment.
Each of the student has completed the assignment.

questions.explanation: 'Each' is singular and governs the verb — 'each ... has'. Option A uses plural 'have' which wrongly agrees with 'students' rather than with 'each' — the classic trap. Option D has 'each of the student' — 'of the' must be followed by a plural noun. Similar pattern: 'everyone has', 'none has' (traditional) / 'none have' (modern).
questions.subject: English

options.option_text: He is more taller than his brother.
He is taller than his brother.
He is more tall than his brother.
He is the tallest than his brother.

questions.explanation: Comparative of 'tall' is 'taller'. Using 'more' with an '-er' form is a double comparative — wrong. 'Tallest' is the superlative and pairs with 'of' or 'in', not 'than'. Rule: short adjectives form comparatives with '-er' (taller, smaller); longer adjectives with 'more' (more beautiful).

questions.stem: Choose the sentence with the correct preposition.

options.option_text: She is married with a doctor.
She is married to a doctor.
She is married from a doctor.
She is married for a doctor.

questions.explanation: 'Married to' is the fixed usage. Other fixed pairs: divorced from, differ from (unlike) / differ with (disagree), congratulate on, prefer to (not 'than'), consist of, depend on, deprive of, replace with.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses the correct tense?

options.option_text: I am living here since 2010.
I have been living here since 2010.
I have lived here since 2010 onwards.
I lived here since 2010.

questions.explanation: 'Since + point of time' with an ongoing action takes the present perfect continuous: 'have been living'. 'Am living' (present continuous) is wrong with 'since'. 'Onwards' is redundant with 'since'. Trigger words for perfect tenses: since, for, lately, recently, so far, up to now.

questions.stem: Which is the correctly formed sentence?

options.option_text: One of my friend is a doctor.
One of my friends is a doctor.
One of my friends are a doctor.
One of my friend are a doctor.

questions.explanation: 'One of + plural noun + singular verb'. 'One of my friends' (must be plural) 'is' (verb agrees with 'one', not with 'friends'). Similar structures: 'one of the books', 'one of the reasons'. Common trap — examiners swap in plural verb 'are' to match 'friends', but the subject is still 'one'.
questions.subject: English

options.option_text: The committee, who met yesterday has approved the plan.
The committee, which met yesterday, has approved the plan.
The committee who met yesterday, has approved the plan.
The committee that met, yesterday has approved the plan.

questions.explanation: Use 'which' (non-human) — 'who' is for people. Non-restrictive clauses are set off by two commas, one on each side. 'Which' is preferred for non-restrictive; 'that' for restrictive (no commas). Option A uses 'who' with a non-person, option D misplaces its comma.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Which sentence uses the correct article?

options.option_text: He is an university professor.
He is a university professor.
He is the university professor.
He is university professor.

questions.explanation: Article choice depends on the sound of the next word, not the spelling. 'University' starts with the consonant sound /ju/, so 'a university'. Same rule: 'a one-rupee coin' (/w/ sound), 'a European' (/j/ sound). Opposite — 'an hour' (silent h → vowel sound), 'an MP' (/em/ sound). Option C (the) is wrong unless pointing to a specific, previously-mentioned professor.
